Launched in 1990, Hubble operates above atmospheric distortion and has produced more than 1.7 million observations, creating a long baseline of high-resolution evidence across ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared wavelengths.

Named in honor of astronomer Edwin Hubble, the telescope's 94.5-inch primary mirror detects light from ultraviolet through near-infrared (115–2500 nanometers), enabling it to peer back 13.4 billion light-years to the early universe. At 43.5 feet long and traveling at 17,000 mph, it completes one orbit every 95 minutes.

Five astronaut servicing missions replaced and upgraded instruments over the telescope's lifetime, keeping it at the cutting edge of science. Its current instruments — the Advanced Camera for Surveys, Cosmic Origins Spectrograph, Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph, and Wide Field Camera 3 — have contributed to more than 22,000 peer-reviewed scientific papers. Hubble has watched a comet collide with Jupiter, discovered moons around Pluto, and probed the supermassive black holes that lurk at the centers of galaxies.

Launched in 2021, Webb is a cryogenic infrared observatory at the Sun-Earth L2 point that extends observable history deeper into early galaxy formation and improves measurement of planetary-system chemistry.

Webb's 6.5-metre primary mirror is made up of 18 gold-coated beryllium segments, folded origami-style to fit inside an Ariane 5 rocket and deployed in space. Each segment is aligned to 1/10,000th the thickness of a human hair, allowing all 18 to act as a single giant mirror with a clear aperture of 25 m².

A five-layer Kapton sunshield measuring 21.197 m × 14.162 m keeps the cold side of the spacecraft below 50 K (−370 °F), a temperature difference of nearly 600 degrees Fahrenheit across its 4.8-metre height. Webb's four instruments — NIRCam, NIRSpec, MIRI, and FGS/NIRISS — are designed to search for the first galaxies formed after the Big Bang, trace the evolution of galaxies over time, observe star and planetary system formation, and measure the atmospheric chemistry of worlds beyond our solar system.

Launched in 1999, Chandra established a new standard for X-ray astronomy by combining high angular resolution with deep sensitivity, enabling precise study of high-energy environments that are invisible in ordinary optical light.

Because X-ray photons penetrate conventional mirrors rather than reflecting from them, Chandra's four pairs of mirrors are shaped like glass barrels and aligned nearly parallel to incoming X-rays so the photons graze off the surface. Polished at Raytheon Optical Systems to the smoothness of a few atoms, the mirrors were then coated with iridium — a rare, highly reflective metal — at Optical Coating Laboratories in California.

The completed mirrors were assembled into a High Resolution Mirror Assembly at Eastman Kodak in Rochester, New York, aligned end-to-end across 2.7 metres to an accuracy of 1.3 micrometers — roughly one-fiftieth the width of a human hair. Chandra is managed by NASA's Marshall Center and operated from the Chandra X-ray Center (CXC) at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, giving scientists worldwide the ability to image the extreme environments where matter is heated to millions of degrees by powerful magnetic fields, intense gravity, and explosive forces.
